title: Going overseas: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and America — go there first to get big
dek: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.
why: Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas investment experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers, and the second half on AI transforming organisations and pricing is the most information-dense.
who: Founders building or preparing overseas brands, cross-border e-commerce operators, and early-stage investors watching consumer going overseas.
skip: The opening pleasantries and 15th-anniversary congratulations, about 1 minute, can be skipped.

points.h: The old cross-border mega-seller path is a dead end
points.body: Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset, with dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. Ten years ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and many investors liked them. But a distribution-style company is essentially a traffic-style company: the more stores, the more likely to get traffic. When platform goods aren't plentiful enough, distribution isn't opposed; once goods are plentiful enough, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, three red lines: goods not matching descriptions harms consumers, brushing orders harms other merchants, and putting in little cards to build private domains harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel places great importance on consumer experience, and these behaviours hit exactly that protective wall.

points.h: Of the four choices, region comes first
points.body: Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce; all of life is about choices being more important than effort. He gives four choices: region choice, channel choice, product category choice, brand positioning choice. On region choice he has always advocated seizing the European and American markets first, because of strong paying power, high internet penetration, and more importantly the brand can build momentum. This isn't something they invented; when Japanese and Korean brands went global back then, they all seized Europe and America. On category choice they change their advice every three years: the earliest three years supported products common to China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification, like Anker's power banks which were almost identical except for voltage; the second three years they advised overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had all gone overseas and common products had no differentiation; the most recent three years is product 3.0 — electric, with chips, with algorithms.

points.h: It's not that you go to Europe and America after getting big, it's that you go there to get big
points.body: Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to Europe and America when I'm big’, and he says it's exactly the reverse — you go to Europe and America to get big. He gives the example of Cupshe, a swimwear company: a husband and wife, stocked $50,000 of goods, and their first stop was the US. $50,000 is goods for sale, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. He recently looked at AI smart hardware, starting from Kickstarter crowdfunding with a thousand or ten thousand products, even taking pre-orders before placing orders, with no capital — this is also a great way to test the waters. He even advises big companies entering the European and American markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce in, and both big and small companies should first do the four singles well: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

points.h: After AI, good companies don't just find demand, they create it
points.body: Wei Zhe says with AI, excellent companies don't go looking for demand, they should lead demand and create demand. He gives the example of a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally not electric, they electrified it, with chips and algorithms; the algorithm is actually very simple, with GPS positioning, and the map of the universe's movements is regular. He wasn't an astronomy enthusiast but would buy one, click once at home in Silicon Valley, it automatically aligns Orion for you, tells you 3 a.m. is the best time, you press it and go to sleep, and the next day it has taken the photos for you. This lets everyone become a good astronomy enthusiast. Another example is a cross-border class student doing curtains: after electrifying them they didn't sell well in the US because American electricians are expensive, so he put solar panels on the windows, turning electric curtains that needed an electrician into DIY ones; originally always one or two hundred million, now four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

points.h: In the AI era, still using subscription fees means you're behind
points.body: Wei Zhe says in the AI era, if you still have the subscription-fee mindset you're behind again; they are all advising companies to do back-end charging, software charging, called tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest way, a bit like advertising charging by time rather than by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, isn't subscribing for a month wasting two weeks? They advise that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not going back to the old SaaS monthly $9.9 subscription model. An AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and doesn't charge if you don't read; the same with smart bike trainers, after topping up it's $1 per ride, $2 for two hours.

points.h: Adding AI is more worth favouring than AI plus
points.body: Wei Zhe has a view called AI plus or plus AI; he reverses the phrase and favours plus AI rather than today favouring AI plus. The difference is: plus AI is hardware humans have already accepted, which you AI-ify; rather than creating a hardware never seen before because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept a completely new hardware. For example, Oura makes rings, because you first accepted rings; some things that hang a camera under your neck are harder for me, I haven't accepted that hardware. So they are very bullish on adding AI to already-accepted hardware. They invested in a capacitive stylus that is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad, it doesn't add an extra pen for you, it just AI-ifies your pen. He also especially wants to transform one of the top one or two overseas fitness equipment companies, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with AI-generated ones — you want a man, it's a man, you want a black person, it's a black person, and with two cameras it can guide your workout with AI.

points.h: Channels aren't flat, they're a pyramid
points.body: Wei Zhe says channels aren't multiple channels multiple paths, each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and which channel new products launch in first all have their rules. What is a light-goods channel, what is the main waist volume channel, the pyramid design differs for different categories and brands. He gives Anker: making power bank mecha seems a bit low, to enter the consumer electronics high ground of Soundcore earphones you have to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot isn't important, but it can transform the brand, Apple is the pyramid's tip. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street, even if it doesn't make money how much can it lose, but it must hold up there. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels for selling goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light-goods channel, when Amazon delists you, dump it in that channel, you can't sell on Amazon and here too, consumers get confused.

Wei Zhe says he really dislikes splashing out on marketing expenses. Many Chinese brands going overseas or cross-border e-commerce are very willing to add 2% of revenue to marketing expenses, but consumers don't get it. He says do you dare add 2% of revenue to R&D expenses. He has met many bosses at the 1 billion or 2 billion scale; at 1 billion they say 20 million for R&D, I don't know what for. He says see, there's the problem, you don't know what for. Your 2% thrown at marketing expenses makes the platform happy, consumers don't get it; but 2% thrown into R&D consumers get it. He has always firmly believed good products speak for themselves, marketing is just, your R&D is 1, marketing is 0, if you have something good you can amplify it, if you don't have that 1 never put many 0s. He gives three judgment signals: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and you crush it by doubling performance; second, you sell at the same price as it; third, you sell online and hit offline channels to come to you.

points.h: AI doesn't just change products, it transforms every role
points.body: Wei Zhe says AI has two important things for enterprises, big, medium and small all must do well: first, the combination of products with AI; second, how the organisation changes through AI. He sees cross-border e-commerce companies as almost the industry among all he has seen that most should use AI to transform every role. Every role asks itself what AI can do for you: product selection, content generation, ad placement choices, essentially all algorithms; previously relying on human experience, and experience is definitely not as strong as algorithmic iteration. Customer service AI-ified, no more customer service, customer service is just you training your customer service agent; ad placement you train an agent; product selection, product display, product image and video generation all AI-ified. He says this is the first and only industry he has seen so far where the entire company's organisational chain can all be transformed by AI. He also says what they most oppose is putting many people overseas, with or without AI they oppose it, called no unnecessary overseas staffing.

points.h: Not just let AI do the work, but let it participate in decisions
points.body: Wei Zhe explains AI and organisation very simply: many companies have P series and M series, P is professional, M is management. Many people are used to letting AI do P, doing the work, generating images which was originally a P-series job. But truly formidable companies don't just let AI do P-series work, they gradually let it do the work of Manager, Director, VP. He gives a real case of AI pricing: the company originally wanted to sell at €35, AI said you can sell at €55, the company really went to €55, it really sold, volume similar to before at €35, but earning €20 more. He says AI has no courage, it's bolder than you, it has compared everything across the whole web for you. He also says even if AI hallucinates, with so many large models in China and the US, they won't all dream the same dream at the same time, so you must cross-validate.

terms.def: Wei Zhe's term for a charging model based on AI usage, replacing monthly subscriptions.
A term Wei Zhe coined: daring to define a price and not lowering it, and when peers catch up to the same performance, competing on performance.
Single market, single category, single channel, single brand — Wei Zhe advises overseas companies to focus first.
Wei Zhe's overseas category advice: from non-electric to electric, electric with chips, chips with AI algorithms.
